title: One Index for Both the Filter and the Sort
description: A screen that both filters and sorts scans then sorts; one composite index (filter column, then sort column in its direction) serves both in a single seek. Why it matters: "filter + sort" (status screens, activity feeds, admin panels) is one of the most common query shapes in production software -- one right index serves both needs at once.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Probably the single most common query shape in ordinary business software is 'show me the newest N things matching some condition' — the newest open support tickets, the most recent active orders, the latest unread notifications, the top items in an admin queue. Every one of these is really the same pattern in disguise: a **filter** (some equality condition, like `Status = 'Open'`) combined with a **sort** (usually by a date or timestamp, newest first) plus a **limit** (show me the top 50, or one page's worth). Understanding how to build exactly the right index for this shape is one of the most broadly useful, most frequently applicable skills in everyday SQL Server tuning, because this pattern is everywhere.

With no supporting index at all, SQL Server has genuinely no good options: it has to read through the entire table (a Clustered Index Scan, touching every single row regardless of status), check each row's `Status` to see if it's `'Open'`, keep the ones that pass, and then — because none of that filtering process produced the rows in `CreatedAt` order — perform an explicit **Sort** on whatever survived the filter, before finally taking just the top 50 off the front of the sorted result. Two completely separate demands (filter, then order) are both going unmet, and the query pays the full cost of both: a full scan for the filter, and a full sort of whatever's left over.

The key insight that makes the fix clean is that a single, well-designed **composite index** — an index built on more than one column — can satisfy *both* demands simultaneously, in a single pass, with no separate sort step needed at all. The trick is in how you order the index's key columns: put the **equality-filter column(s) first**, and the **sort column(s) second, in the exact direction the sort needs**. So for `WHERE Status = 'Open' ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC`, the right index is `(Status, CreatedAt DESC)`.

To see why this ordering works, think about what that index physically looks like once built: rows are grouped together by `Status` first (all the 'Open' rows sit together, contiguous, separate from all the 'Closed' or 'Cancelled' rows), and *within* each status group, rows are stored sorted by `CreatedAt`, newest-first because the index was declared `DESC` on that column. Now when the query runs, SQL Server can do a single **Index Seek** straight to the start of the `'Open'` group — skipping every row belonging to any other status entirely, the same way an index lets you skip straight to a specific letter in a phone book — and because the rows within that group are *already* stored newest-first, it can just read the first 50 rows it finds and stop. There's no separate sorting step required at all, because the physical storage order the index provides already matches the exact order the query wants. The filter and the sort are both satisfied by the very same single read.

The direction matters here in exactly the way covered in this course's dedicated lesson on mixed ASC/DESC sorts: if you built the index as `(Status, CreatedAt)` — both ascending, the default — it would still let you seek to the `'Open'` group efficiently, but within that group the rows would be stored oldest-first, the opposite of what the `ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC` wants, so SQL Server would still need a Sort step afterward (just a much cheaper one, since it's only sorting the 'Open' rows rather than the whole table). Declaring the index's second column as `DESC` to begin with removes even that residual sort, because 'newest first' is baked directly into how the rows are physically stored on disk.

Why is this exact pattern — one equality filter, one sort column, one small limit — so universal in real applications? Because almost every list-style screen in business software works this way: show me things in some status, newest (or highest-priority, or soonest-due) first, and only the first page of them, because nobody scrolls through thousands of rows — they look at the top 20 or 50 and move on. Status dashboards, activity feeds, admin task queues, notification lists, recent-orders widgets — all of them share this exact filter-plus-sort-plus-limit shape, which means that once you've internalized 'equality columns first, sort columns second in the sort's direction' as a rule, you can apply it directly to a huge fraction of the slow list-screen queries you'll ever encounter in a real system.

What to look for in a plan with this problem: a full table or Clustered Index Scan feeding into an explicit **Sort**, which then feeds into a **Top** operator — that specific shape (scan, then sort, then take just the first few rows) is the signature of 'this query is filtering and sorting with no index doing either job for it.' The fix is to build a composite index with the filter column(s) first and the sort column(s) second in matching direction, and — for maximum benefit — `INCLUDE` whatever other columns the query needs to display, so the index becomes fully covering and the query never needs to visit the base table at all.

## Scenario
A task screen shows the 50 newest `Open` tasks: `WHERE Status = 'Open' ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC`. With no supporting index, SQL Server reads the whole table, filters, and then sorts what's left — to return 50 rows.

## Why it's slow
Two demands — a **filter** on `Status` and an **ordering** by `CreatedAt DESC` — and nothing to satisfy either. The plan is a Clustered Index Scan plus an explicit **Sort**. The right index answers both at once: filter *and* order.

## What to look for
- A Clustered Index Scan feeding a Sort, then a Top.
- A query that both filters and sorts, with no single index covering the pair.

## The concept
Build the index as **filter column(s) first, then sort column(s) in the sort's direction**: `(Status, CreatedAt DESC)`. SQL Server seeks to `Status = 'Open'` and, because those rows are already stored newest-first, reads the top 50 in order — **no Sort**. A well-ordered composite index can serve an equality filter and an `ORDER BY` in a single seek. INCLUDE the displayed columns to keep it covering.
startingQuery:
SELECT TOP (50) TaskId, Title, CreatedAt
FROM Tasks
WHERE Status = 'Open'
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC;
hints: Nothing supports the Status filter or the CreatedAt ordering, so the table is scanned and then sorted.
You want one index that seeks the filtered rows already in the sort order -- equality column first, sort column (in its direction) next.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Tasks_Status_Created ON Tasks(Status, CreatedAt DESC) INCLUDE (Title); then re-run.
